mainTopic: Believing a father about his בכור (רבי יהודה vs. the רבנן on 'יכיר'), and believing a man who calls someone his son or his slave
overview: This amud opens with the end of שמואל's ruling and asks why he blended two opinions instead of picking one; the answer is that he was unsure whether the הלכה follows רבי יהודה or the רבנן. The גמרא then quotes the ברייתא on 'יכיר': רבי יהודה says a father is believed to name his בכור, and even to say a son is a בן גרושה or בן חלוצה, while the חכמים say he is not believed. The גמרא asks why the רבנן need the word 'יכיר', and explains that it covers a case where nobody knows who the בכור is. It is needed for property the father gets later, or, for רבי מאיר, property that comes while he is a גוסס, since he could not give that as a gift. A ברייתא about a father going against what people assume about the בכור is split between רבי יהודה and the רבנן. רבי יוחנן then teaches when a man is believed after calling someone 'my son' or 'my slave', and the rule flips at the tax house. A ברייתא challenges him, and רב נחמן בר יצחק answers that it is about someone publicly known as 'a slave worth a hundred'. Finally, רבי אבא sends a case about a disputed slave, and its ruling continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The closing words of שמואל's answer
steps.stepSummary: The words 'each to the other' finish the answer שמואל sent back, which started just before this section.
steps.simpleTranslation: …each to the other.
steps.whatsHappening: These two words are the end of שמואל's reply to the question that was sent to him. His ruling ends with the two parties acting toward each other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing new is argued here; this simply completes שמואל's ruling. The important point is that his answer is built so that each side acts toward the other, instead of picking one clear winner. That shape is what the גמרא is about to question.

keyTerms.meaning: each to the other; one toward the other

phrases.english: each to the other.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes שמואל's ruling, which began before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שמואל ruled that the two parties act each toward the other, a ruling that does not follow just one תנא.

steps.title: Why didn't שמואל pick one side?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges שמואל: whichever opinion he holds, he should have ruled clearly according to it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whichever way you look at it: if he agrees with the רבנן, he should have sent them an answer like the רבנן. If he agrees with רבי יהודה, he should have sent them an answer like רבי יהודה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks שמואל's mixed ruling. It argues that he must hold one view or the other, so he should simply have answered according to that view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge uses a 'מה נפשך' structure, which means 'either way, there is a problem.' Both possible positions lead to the same complaint: a clear ruling was expected, not a blend. The hidden assumption is that a פוסק always knows which side he agrees with.

keyTerms.meaning: whichever way you want it; either way there is a problem
he holds; he agrees with
let him send them; he should have sent them
the Rabbis; the majority of חכמים

phrases.english: Whichever way you look at it?
If he holds like the Rabbis,
he should send them an answer like the Rabbis;
if he holds like Rabbi Yehuda,
he should send them an answer like Rabbi Yehuda!

steps.triggerLanguage: מָה נַפְשָׁךְ? אִי כְּרַבָּנַן סְבִירָא לֵיהּ, לִישְׁלַח לְהוּ כְּרַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions why the ruling just quoted blends both opinions.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A dilemma: whether שמואל holds like the רבנן or like רבי יהודה, he should have ruled plainly according to that view, not given a mixed answer.

steps.title: שמואל was unsure which view is the הלכה
steps.stepSummary: שמואל was in doubt whether the הלכה follows רבי יהודה or the רבנן, so his ruling works under both.
steps.simpleTranslation: He was unsure whether the הלכה is like רבי יהודה or like the רבנן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. שמואל did not hold either view for sure; he was in doubt, so he gave a ruling that is safe under both.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This removes the assumption behind the קשיא, that שמואל must have decided. Once he is in doubt, a blended ruling is not confused but careful. It protects both sides whichever opinion turns out to be the הלכה.

keyTerms.meaning: he is in doubt; he is unsure

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows a common way a פוסק handles a real doubt between two תנאים: he rules in a way that holds up under both views, instead of guessing.

phrases.english: He is unsure
whether it is like Rabbi Yehuda or like the Rabbis.

steps.triggerLanguage: מְסַפְּקָא לֵיהּ אִי כְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה אִי כְּרַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'מה נפשך' challenge.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rejects the challenge's assumption: שמואל had not decided between the two views.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We assumed שמואל must agree with one of the two opinions, so a mixed ruling made no sense.
steps.terutzMaskana: שמואל was in doubt, so he deliberately ruled in a way that works under both opinions.

steps.title: What is this מחלוקת?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what exactly the disagreement between רבי יהודה and the רבנן is.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the source of the מחלוקת it just mentioned. This sets up the next step, where a ברייתא is quoted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the גמרא only named the two sides. To understand why שמואל was in doubt, we need to see what each side actually says.

keyTerms.meaning: what is it? (asking for the source or details)

phrases.english: What is it?
phrases.notes: He's asking: what's the disagreement between רבי יהודה and the רבנן that we just mentioned?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the details of the מחלוקת referred to in the answer.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source and content of the disagreement between רבי יהודה and the רבנן.

steps.title: The ברייתא on 'יכיר': a father identifies his firstborn
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא reads the פסוק 'יכיר' to mean that a father can identify his בכור to others.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught in a ברייתא: 'He shall acknowledge' means he shall identify him to others.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins answering by quoting a ברייתא. It learns from the word 'יכיר' that a father may tell other people which son is his firstborn.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says the father must 'acknowledge' the בכור. The ברייתא reads this as giving the father the power to identify him to others, so people may rely on his word. This is the start of the source where רבי יהודה and the רבנן will disagree.

keyTerms.meaning: as it was taught in a ברייתא
he shall acknowledge (דברים כא:יז)
he shall identify him to others
firstborn son, who gets a double portion of the inheritance

phrases.english: As it is taught: 'He shall acknowledge,'
he shall identify him to others.
phrases.notes: The father tells other people which son is his firstborn, and they may rely on him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts answering 'מאי היא' by quoting the ברייתא.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The ברייתא learns from 'יכיר' that a father can identify his firstborn to others. The rest of the ברייתא, with the מחלוקת itself, comes in step 6.

steps.title: רבי יהודה and the חכמים argue over a father's believability
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues. From 'יכיר', רבי יהודה learns that a father is believed to name his בכור, and also to say a son is a בן גרושה or בן חלוצה. The חכמים say he is not believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: From here רבי יהודה said: a man is believed to say 'This is my firstborn son.' Just as he is believed about that, he is also believed to say 'This is the son of a divorced woman' or 'This is the son of a חלוצה.' The חכמים say: he is not believed.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא from the last step finishes. It shows us the exact argument between רבי יהודה and the חכמים, which is what the גמרא asked about in step 4.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה stretches the father's believability beyond the בכור. A כהן father can also make his son lose כהונה by saying the mother was a גרושה or a חלוצה. The חכמים reject the father's believability.

keyTerms.meaning: believed; his word is accepted
firstborn son, who gets a double share of the inheritance
son of a כהן and a divorced woman; he is a חלל and not a כהן
son of a כהן and a woman who did חליצה; he is also not a full כהן
the Sages, the majority opinion (here, the same as the רבנן)

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יהודה: the father is believed (בכור, בן גרושה, בן חלוצה). חכמים: he is not believed.

phrases.english: From here Rabbi Yehuda said:
A person is believed to say:
"This is my firstborn son."
And just as a person is believed to say
"This is my firstborn son,"
so too a person is believed to say
"This is the son of a divorced woman"
phrases.notes: This is a כהן father talking. Saying this means his son loses כהונה.

phrases.english: and "This is the son of a woman who did חליצה."
And the Sages say: He is not believed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא started in step 5 and gives the answer to step 4's question.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What exactly do רבי יהודה and the רבנן disagree about?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי יהודה says a father is believed about his בכור and about a son being a בן גרושה or בן חלוצה. The חכמים say he is not believed.

steps.title: Why do the רבנן need the word 'יכיר'?
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק asks רבא a question. For רבי יהודה, 'יכיר' is the source for the father's believability. But the רבנן say he is not believed, so what is the word there for?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said to רבא: It makes sense for רבי יהודה, since that is why the פסוק says 'יכיר'. But for the רבנן, why do I need 'יכיר'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the רבנן. Their opinion seems to leave the word 'יכיר' with no job.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A word in the תורה is expected to teach something. רבי יהודה uses 'יכיר' to teach that the father is believed. Since the רבנן say he is not believed, it looks like the word teaches them nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: it makes sense / granted (opens a 'this works, but that doesn't' challenge)
'he shall identify', the פסוק about the father and his בכור
why do I need it?

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק לְרָבָא:
phrases.english: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said to Rava:
It makes sense according to Rabbi Yehuda
that is why it is written: "He shall identify."
But according to the Rabbis,
why do I need "he shall identify"?

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא לְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה הַיְינוּ דִּכְתִיב יַכִּיר אֶלָּא לְרַבָּנַן יַכִּיר לְמָה לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the חכמים's opinion from step 6.
steps.kashyaTarget: The opinion of the רבנן/חכמים that the father is not believed.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the father is not believed, the word 'יכיר' seems to have no purpose.

steps.title: 'יכיר' is for when nobody knows who the בכור is
steps.stepSummary: For the רבנן, 'יכיר' teaches that the father is believed when nobody knows which son is the בכור.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed for a case where identification is needed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers for the רבנן. It gives the word 'יכיר' a smaller job that the רבנן can agree with.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבנן only disagree when another son is already known as the בכור. When no one knows, even the רבנן agree the father is believed. That is what 'יכיר' teaches.

keyTerms.meaning: identification; knowing who someone is

steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean the רבנן now agree with רבי יהודה. They only accept the father's word when no son is already known as the בכור.

phrases.english: Where identification is needed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 7.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the פסוק to a narrower case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: For the רבנן, 'יכיר' seemed to teach nothing.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'יכיר' teaches that the father is believed when no son is already known as the בכור.

steps.title: What does the father's word accomplish? He could just give a gift
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what law the father's believability would matter for. If it is the double share, the פסוק isn't needed: the father could give that son extra money as a gift anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: For what law? To give him a double share? Let him be no better than any other person: if the father wanted to give it to him as a gift, couldn't he give it to him?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer of step 8. It asks what practical difference the father's word would make.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The double share is the main law of a בכור. But a father can give money as a gift to anyone, even a stranger. So he could give this son the extra share without the פסוק, and a פסוק just to teach that seems unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: for what law? / what difference does it make?
a double share of the inheritance
a gift
let it be no more than

phrases.english: For what law?
To give him a double share?
Let him be no better than another person
phrases.notes: Even a total stranger can receive the father's money if the father gives it as a gift.

phrases.english: if he wanted to give it to him as a gift,
could he not give it to him?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that 'יכיר' teaches the father is believed when nobody knows who the בכור is.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A father can give anyone money as a gift, so the double share doesn't need the father to be believed. A פסוק for that seems pointless.

steps.title: The verse is needed for property the father gets later
steps.stepSummary: 'יכיר' is needed for property that comes to the father after he names his בכור. He could not have given that property as a gift beforehand.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the verse is needed for property that came to him afterward.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from Step 9. The verse is needed for property the father only gets later, after he names his son as the בכור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A gift only works on property you already own. So property that comes to the father after he speaks cannot be handed over as a gift at that time. Only the father being believed through 'יכיר' gives that son a double share of it.

keyTerms.meaning: It is only needed for (a specific case)
Property that came into his possession
Afterward, from now on

phrases.english: No, it is needed
for property that came to him afterward.
phrases.notes: He means after the father said which son is the בכור. You can't give away as a gift something you don't own yet.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 9 that a gift would make the verse unneeded.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case: the verse is needed where a gift is impossible.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The father could give the double share as a gift anyway, so 'יכיר' adds nothing.
steps.terutzMaskana: For property the father acquires later, no gift was possible, so 'יכיר' is needed.

steps.title: For רבי מאיר, why is the verse needed?
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר holds that a person can transfer something that does not exist yet. For him, the father could give even future property as a gift, so why is 'יכיר' needed?
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to רבי מאיר, who says a person can transfer ownership of something that has not yet come into the world, why do I need 'יכיר'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer of Step 10 using the view of רבי מאיר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 10's answer relied on the rule that you cannot give away what you don't own yet. רבי מאיר disagrees: he says a person can transfer something that has not come into the world. For him, the father could give future property as a gift too, so the original question returns.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא whose view is quoted here
Transfers ownership
Something that does not yet exist or is not yet his
Why do I need it?

phrases.english: And according to רבי מאיר, who says:
a person can transfer ownership of a thing
that has not come into the world,
why do I need 'he shall acknowledge'?
phrases.notes: This is the word from the פסוק in דברים 21:17 that the whole discussion is about.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְרַבִּי מֵאִיר, דְּאָמַר: אָדָם מַקְנֶה דָּבָר שֶׁלֹּא בָּא לָעוֹלָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks Step 10's answer from the view of a different תנא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that 'יכיר' is needed for property acquired later.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: For רבי מאיר, even future property can be given as a gift, so the verse is again unneeded.

steps.title: Property that came while the father was dying
steps.stepSummary: Even for רבי מאיר, 'יכיר' is needed for property that came to the father while he was a גוסס.
steps.simpleTranslation: For property that came to him while he was a גוסס.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that even רבי מאיר needs the verse, for property that comes to the father when he is at the very end of his life.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A גוסס can no longer give gifts. So property that reaches him at that point cannot be handed over as a gift, even according to רבי מאיר. Only the father being believed through 'יכיר' gives the בכור his double share of it.

keyTerms.meaning: A person in his final moments of life

steps.whatToRemember: For both views, 'יכיר' is needed for property the father could never have given as a gift. For those who hold you cannot give away what you don't own yet, that is property that comes later. For רבי מאיר, it is property that comes while he is a גוסס.

phrases.english: For property that came to him
when he was dying.
phrases.notes: At this stage he can't give gifts anymore, so a gift could not have worked here.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from רבי מאיר's view in Step 11.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case to a situation where no gift is possible even for רבי מאיר.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: For רבי מאיר any property can be given as a gift, so 'יכיר' is unneeded.
steps.terutzMaskana: Property that came while the father was a גוסס cannot be given, so 'יכיר' is needed.

steps.title: A father's word against what people assume about the firstborn
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא: if one son is assumed to be the בכור and the father names another son, the father is believed. If a son is assumed not to be the בכור and the father says he is, the father is not believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: If people assumed about a son that he is the בכור, and his father said about another son that he is the בכור, the father is believed. If people assumed about a son that he is not the בכור, and his father said he is the בכור, the father is not believed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about when a father's statement can go against an existing assumption about who the בכור is. This sets up the next discussion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two cases seem to pull in opposite directions. In the first, the father's word overrides the assumption, but in the second it does not. Keep both cases clearly in mind, since the גמרא will need to explain how they fit together.

keyTerms.meaning: The Sages taught (introduces a ברייתא)
Held to be, presumed (a חזקה)
Firstborn son, who gets a double share
Believed, trusted

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
If they presumed about him that he is the firstborn,
and his father said about another son
that he is the firstborn, he is believed.
If they presumed about him that he is not the firstborn,
and his father said: He is the firstborn,
he is not believed.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הָיוּ מוּחְזָקִין בּוֹ שֶׁהוּא בְּכוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After finishing the discussion of why 'יכיר' is needed, the גמרא brings a new ברייתא about a father's believability against an existing חזקה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A father is believed to name a different son as בכור against an assumption, but not to make a son the בכור when people assume he is not.

steps.title: The two halves of the ברייתא follow different opinions
steps.stepSummary: The first half of the ברייתא, where the father is believed, follows רבי יהודה. The second half, where he is not believed, follows the רבנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: The first part of the ברייתא is רבי יהודה, and the last part is the רבנן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the two halves of the ברייתא from the last step seem to go against each other. Each half follows a different תנא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first half the father is believed to change who the בכור is, which fits רבי יהודה's reading of 'יכיר.' In the second half he is not believed, which fits the רבנן, who do not give the father that power. So the ברייתא is not contradicting itself. It is mixing two opinions.

keyTerms.meaning: The first part of a teaching
The last part of a teaching
The תנא who holds the father is believed based on 'יכיר'
The Sages, the majority opinion

steps.whatToRemember: When two halves of one ברייתא clash, the גמרא may say each half follows a different תנא.

phrases.english: The first clause is Rabbi Yehuda,
phrases.notes: This is the ברייתא from the last step, about the son everyone assumed was the בכור, where the father names a different son.

phrases.english: and the latter clause is the Rabbis.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the clash between the two halves of the ברייתא brought in Step 13
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the ברייתא between two תנאים
steps.terutzHavaAmina: One might think the ברייתא follows a single opinion and contradicts itself
steps.terutzMaskana: The first half is רבי יהודה and the second half is the רבנן

steps.title: Saying 'my son' and then 'my slave,' or the other way around
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן: if someone says 'he is my son' and then 'he is my slave,' he is not believed. If he says 'my slave' and then 'my son,' he is believed, because 'my slave' only meant 'he serves me like a slave.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: If a man said 'He is my son' and then said 'He is my slave,' he is not believed. If he said 'He is my slave' and then said 'He is my son,' he is believed, because by 'my slave' he meant 'he serves me like a slave.'
steps.whatsHappening: A new teaching begins. רבי יוחנן tells us when a man can take back what he said about someone being his son or his slave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once he calls the person 'my son,' he cannot take that back and later turn him into a slave. 'My son' has no loose meaning that would explain it away. But 'my slave' can be read loosely as 'he works for me like a slave,' so the later claim 'he is my son' does not truly contradict it, and he is believed.

keyTerms.meaning: A leading אמורא of ארץ ישראל
And then he said again, changing his words
Believed
Serves, works for someone

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan says:
If one said: 'He is my son,'
and then said: 'He is my slave' –
he is not believed.
'He is my slave,' and then said 'He is my son' – he is believed,
since he was saying: 'He serves me like a slave.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic about being believed on personal status, beyond the בכור
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'Son' then 'slave' is not believed. 'Slave' then 'son' is believed, because 'slave' can mean 'serves me like a slave.'

steps.title: At the tax house the rule is reversed
steps.stepSummary: Passing a tax house, if he says 'my son' and later 'my slave,' he is believed. If he says 'my slave' and later 'my son,' he is not believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: The reverse is true at the tax house. If he was passing the tax house and said 'He is my son,' and later said 'He is my slave,' he is believed. If he said 'He is my slave,' and later said 'He is my son,' he is not believed.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן's teaching continues with a case where the rule flips: at a tax house.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At the tax house a man has a reason to call his slave 'my son,' because slaves were taxed there. So the first claim 'my son' is easy to explain away, and the later 'my slave' is believed. But nobody would call his son 'my slave' there and pay a tax for nothing, so 'my slave' sticks.

keyTerms.meaning: And the reverse of it
The tax house, a customs post

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that whether a person is believed depends on whether his first words had a clear reason behind them other than the truth.

phrases.english: And the reverse applies at the tax house –
if he was passing the tax house
and said: 'He is my son,'
phrases.notes: Slaves were taxed at the tax house, so calling a slave 'my son' would let him skip the tax.

phrases.english: and then said: 'He is my slave' – he is believed.
If he said: 'He is my slave,'
and then said: 'He is my son' – he is not believed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רבי יוחנן's teaching with the reverse case at the tax house
steps.mimraCoreRuling: At the tax house, 'son' then 'slave' is believed, and 'slave' then 'son' is not believed.

steps.title: A ברייתא says 'slave' then 'son' is not believed
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that if someone served him like a slave, and he said 'my slave' and then 'my son,' he is not believed. This seems to go against רבי יוחנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged: If someone was serving him like a son, and he came and said 'He is my son' and then said 'He is my slave,' he is not believed. If someone was serving him like a slave, and he came and said 'He is my slave' and then said 'He is my son,' he is not believed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to challenge רבי יוחנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first case matches רבי יוחנן: 'son' then 'slave' is not believed. But the second case says 'slave' then 'son' is also not believed, while רבי יוחנן said that case is believed. That is the contradiction.

keyTerms.meaning: They challenged, raising an objection from a ברייתא
Serving him the way a son serves
Serving him the way a slave serves

steps.confusionAlert: The challenge comes only from the second half of the ברייתא. The first half agrees with רבי יוחנן.

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
If one was serving him like a son,
and he came and said: 'He is my son,'
and then said: 'He is my slave' – he is not believed.
If one was serving him like a slave,
and he came and said: 'He is my slave,'
and then said: 'He is my son' – he is not believed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the second ruling of רבי יוחנן in Step 15
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's ruling that 'slave' then 'son' is believed
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא says that in the 'slave' then 'son' case he is not believed, which is the opposite of רבי יוחנן's ruling.

steps.title: The ברייתא is about a slave everyone calls 'a slave worth a hundred'
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק says the ברייתא's case is different from רבי יוחנן's case. In the ברייתא, everyone publicly calls this person 'a slave worth a hundred.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: There, in the ברייתא, it is a case where people call him 'a slave of a hundred.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 17. The ברייתא, where the man is not believed, is a special case: the person is publicly known as a slave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן's rule is about a case where the only thing we have is the man's own words. Then 'my slave' can be read loosely, as 'he serves me like a slave.' In the ברייתא, everyone already treats this person as a real slave. So the man cannot later undo that by saying 'he is my son.' The two sources describe different situations, so they do not argue.

keyTerms.meaning: There, meaning in that other case (here, the ברייתא)
That people call him
A slave
Literally 'bordering a hundred.' A nickname for a slave worth a hundred זוזים

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a public reputation (what everyone says about a person) can count for more than one man's later claim.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said:
There, it is where they call him:
phrases.notes: 'There' points back to the ברייתא from the last step, where the man was not believed.

phrases.english: 'A slave bordering a hundred.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק: הָתָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 17 against רבי יוחנן
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): the ברייתא deals with a slave who has a public reputation as a slave
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to contradict רבי יוחנן's rule that 'my slave' followed by 'my son' is believed
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי יוחנן's rule stands. The ברייתא only covers someone publicly known as a slave.

steps.title: What does 'bordering a hundred' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the nickname 'מצר מאה' means.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is 'bordering a hundred'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses to ask about the strange wording of the nickname. This sets up a short explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a question about wording only. It does not challenge the answer just given; it only wants to understand the phrase.

keyTerms.meaning: What is? (asking for an explanation)

phrases.english: What is 'bordering a hundred'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the meaning of a phrase used in step 18
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning of the nickname 'מצר מאה'

steps.title: A slave worth a hundred זוזים
steps.stepSummary: The nickname means a hundred זוזים 'border' (sit next to) the slave, so he is worth a hundred זוזים.
steps.simpleTranslation: A hundred זוזים border the slave.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that the nickname is about the slave's price: he is worth a hundred זוזים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: People talk about him in terms of his market value, the way people talk about property. That shows how firmly everyone sees him as a real slave.

keyTerms.meaning: זוזים, a type of coin
Borders, sits next to

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יוחנן's rule (that 'my slave' then 'my son' is believed) holds. It does not apply when the person is publicly known as a slave, such as one people call 'a slave worth a hundred.'

phrases.english: A hundred zuz border the slave.
phrases.notes: In other words, he is worth a hundred זוזים.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 19
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: It means the slave is valued at a hundred זוזים

steps.title: רבי אבא's case: 'You stole my slave' and 'You sold him to me'
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא sends a ruling to רב יוסף בר חמא. One man says, 'You stole my slave.' The other says, 'I didn't steal him.' Asked why the slave is with him, he answers, 'You sold him to me.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא sent to רב יוסף בר חמא: Someone says to his friend, 'You stole my slave,' and he answers, 'I did not steal.' 'Then what is he doing with you?' 'You sold him to me.'
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. The גמרא is setting up a case, and the ruling comes in the next part of the text.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both men agree the slave once belonged to the first man. The holder does not say the slave was always his. He claims he bought the slave from the first owner. The question still to come is whether we believe the holder's claim.

keyTerms.meaning: He sent to him (a ruling sent by letter or messenger)
You stole
What is he doing with you? (literally, what is his nature by you)
You sold him

steps.confusionAlert: The text stops in the middle of the case. The ruling (who is believed) has not come yet, so don't look for it here.

phrases.english: Rabbi Abba sent to
Rav Yosef bar Chama:
One who says to his friend: 'You stole my slave,'
and he says: 'I did not steal.'
'What is he doing with you?'
phrases.notes: The first man is asking this; the next line is the other man's answer.

phrases.english: 'You sold him to me;'

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁלַח לֵיהּ רַבִּי אַבָּא לְרַב יוֹסֵף בַּר חָמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the son/slave discussion ends
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The case is being set up: the holder says the owner sold him the slave. The ruling continues in the next part of the text.
